topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: According to the three basic rules of navigation, which principle requires every operator to watch and listen for other vessels and hazards at all times?
explanation: Keep a Proper Lookout requires every operator to use both sight and hearing at all times to watch and listen for other vessels, hazards, and activities.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Under the Navigation Rules, what is the term for the right side of a vessel?
explanation: Right side of a vessel is called starboard; left side is called port.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: When two power-driven vessels are meeting head-on or nearly head-on, what must each vessel do?
choice_a: Alter course to port so each passes starboard to starboard
choice_b: Stop and wait for a sound signal from the other vessel
choice_c: Alter course to starboard so each passes on the port side of the other
choice_d: Maintain course and speed without altering
explanation: In a head-on meeting, each vessel shall alter course to starboard (right) so that each passes on the port side of the other.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Head-on)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel must give way?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other vessel on its port side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel on its starboard side
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel which has the other on her starboard side shall give way and avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Crossing)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In a crossing situation between a power-driven vessel and a sailing vessel under sail, which vessel must give way, regardless of the approach angle?
choice_d: Whichever vessel arrives at the crossing point first
explanation: In crossing situations, power boats must give way to sailing vessels under sail regardless of the angle the power-driven vessel approaches the sailing vessel.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Giveway and Stand-on Vessels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: The 'stand-on' vessel in a crossing or passing situation is expected to:
choice_a: Immediately change course to avoid the other vessel
choice_b: Maintain course and speed unless it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action
choice_c: Sound five short blasts and stop
explanation: The stand-on vessel shall maintain course and speed unless it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Giveway and Stand-on Vessels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: If a stand-on vessel must take action to avoid collision, which turn should it avoid making toward a vessel on its port side?
choice_d: A gradual turn, only sharp turns are allowed
explanation: If the stand-on vessel must take action to avoid a collision, it must avoid turning to port for a vessel on her port side.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Giveway and Stand-on Vessels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel is required to give way?
choice_b: Neither vessel needs to give way
explanation: Any vessel overtaking any other shall give way and keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Overtaking)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: One short blast of a horn during an overtaking maneuver signals what intent?
choice_a: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side
choice_b: I intend to overtake you on your port side
choice_d: I am altering course to port
explanation: One short blast of the horn or whistle means 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side'; two short blasts means the intent to pass on the port side.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Overtaking)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: If a vessel is uncertain whether it is overtaking another vessel, what should it assume?
choice_a: That it is not overtaking, and proceed normally
choice_b: That it is overtaking, and act accordingly
choice_c: That the other vessel will signal first
choice_d: That right-of-way rules do not apply
explanation: When a vessel is in any doubt as to whether it is overtaking another, it shall assume that this is the case and act accordingly.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Overtaking)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: When two sailing vessels approach each other with the wind on different sides, which vessel must keep out of the way?
choice_a: The vessel with the wind on her starboard side
choice_b: The larger of the two vessels
choice_c: The vessel with the wind on her port side
explanation: When each sailing vessel has the wind on a different side, the vessel which has the wind on the port side shall keep out of the way of the other.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessel Crossing)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: When two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, which vessel must keep out of the way?
choice_b: The vessel with the largest sail area
explanation: When both sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the vessel which is to windward shall keep out of the way of the vessel to leeward.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessel Crossing)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: The 'windward' side of a sailing vessel is defined as the side:
choice_a: Opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried
choice_b: On which the mainsail is carried
explanation: Windward side is deemed to be the side opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sailing Vessel Crossing)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A power-driven vessel is required to keep out of the way of which of the following types of vessels?
choice_a: Any other power-driven vessel of equal size
choice_b: A vessel engaged in commercial fishing
choice_c: A PWC operating at no-wake speed
choice_d: A vessel that is anchored in a marked no-anchor zone
explanation: A power-driven vessel shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in commercial fishing, and a sailing vessel.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Responsibility Between Vessels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of which of these, per the Responsibility Between Vessels rule?
choice_b: A vessel operating at no-wake speed
choice_c: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, such as a tug boat or deep-draft freighter
explanation: A sailing vessel shall keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in commercial fishing.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Responsibility Between Vessels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: May an operator ever depart from the standard Navigation Rules?
choice_b: Only with prior DWR written approval
choice_d: Yes, when necessary to avoid immediate danger
explanation: At times it may be necessary to depart from the rules in order to avoid immediate danger; this does not relieve the give-way vessel of its general obligation to keep out of the way.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Departure From Regulations)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In a narrow channel, the operator of a vessel should keep to which side of the fairway or mid-channel when it is safe and practicable?
explanation: In narrow channels, the operator of every vessel shall, when safe and practicable, keep to the side of the fairway or mid-channel that lies on the right side of the vessel.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Narrow Channels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel making way through the water must sound what signal, and how often?
choice_b: One prolonged blast at least once every 2 minutes
choice_d: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts every minute
explanation: A power-driven vessel making way through the water sounds one prolonged blast at least once every 2 minutes in restricted visibility.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sound Signals for Restricted Visibility)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel that is underway but stopped and making no way sounds what signal pattern?
choice_c: Two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_d: No signal is required when stopped
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way sounds two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sound Signals for Restricted Visibility)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: In restricted visibility, a sailing vessel, whether underway or at anchor, sounds what signal at least once every 2 minutes?
choice_d: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
explanation: A sailing vessel, underway or at anchor, sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts at least once every 2 minutes in restricted visibility.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sound Signals for Restricted Visibility)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A 'prolonged blast' as defined in the restricted-visibility sound signal rules lasts how long?
explanation: A prolonged blast is defined as a blast of from 4-6 seconds' duration, while a short blast is about 1 second.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Sound Signals for Restricted Visibility)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: When navigating in restricted visibility and hearing the fog signal of another vessel apparently forward of the beam, what should a vessel do?
choice_a: Increase speed to clear the area quickly
choice_b: Reduce speed to the minimum at which it can be kept on course, and take all way off if necessary
choice_c: Sound five short blasts and hold course
explanation: A vessel hearing apparently forward of her beam the fog signal of another vessel shall reduce speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on course, and if necessary take all way off, navigating with extreme caution.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Restricted Visibility)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Entering a channel or river from open water, buoys marking the starboard side of the channel are what color and numbering?
explanation: Entering a channel or river from open water, buoys on the right (starboard) are painted red and are even numbered starting from the mouth.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Aids to Navigation)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Buoys marking the port side of a channel when entering from open water are what color and numbering scheme?
explanation: Buoys on the left (port) side of the channel are green with odd numbers.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Aids to Navigation)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: What does the mnemonic 'Red Right Returning' mean for a boater navigating a channel?
choice_a: Keep red buoys on your right when returning (heading upstream or in from the ocean)
choice_b: Keep red buoys on your left at all times
choice_c: Turn right whenever you see a red buoy, regardless of direction
choice_d: Red buoys mark hazards to be avoided entirely, not kept to either side
explanation: 'Red Right Returning' means keeping red buoys on your right side when returning, meaning heading upstream or coming in from the ocean.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Aids to Navigation)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A buoy marking a mid-channel is identified by what pattern?
explanation: Buoys marking mid-channel have red and white vertical stripes.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Aids to Navigation)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: A horizontally striped buoy marking an obstruction or junction with a red top band indicates what to the boater?
choice_a: Keep the buoy on your left
choice_c: Keep the buoy on your right
explanation: On horizontally striped obstruction/junction buoys, the top band marks the best channel: a red top means keep the buoy on your right; a green top means keep the buoy on your left.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Aids to Navigation)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Copies of the official Navigation Rules can be obtained from the Superintendent of Documents or which other source mentioned in the guide?
choice_a: The DWR Boat Section by mail only
explanation: Copies of the rules may be obtained from the Superintendent of Documents, U.S. Government Printing Office, or on the USCG website.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: According to the narrow channel rule, a vessel under 65.6 feet in length underway, fishing, or at anchor in a narrow channel must do what?
choice_a: Not interfere with the passage of large, deep-draft vessels that can safely navigate only inside such channels
choice_b: Anchor only at designated mooring buoys
choice_c: Yield to all sailing vessels regardless of size
explanation: The operator of a vessel under 65.6 feet in length underway, fishing, or at anchor in narrow channels shall not interfere with the passage of large, deep-draft vessels that can safely navigate only inside such channels.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules - Narrow Channels)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Which of the three basic navigation rules emphasizes that every operator must take necessary action, in ample time and at a safe distance, to avoid collisions?
explanation: Practice Good Seamanship means it is the responsibility of every operator to take necessary action to avoid collisions, done in ample time and at a safe distance.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules)

topic: VA Boating: Navigation Rules & Aids to Navigation
question: Most boating accidents in Virginia's guide are described as resulting from what type of event?
choice_c: A collision, either between two vessels or between a vessel and a fixed or submerged object
choice_d: Overloading beyond capacity plate limits exclusively
explanation: Most boating accidents are the result of a collision, either between two vessels or between a vessel and a fixed or submerged object.
source_note: VA Boater's Guide - Safe Boating (Navigation Rules)
